object_types.name: Incident
object_types.definition: An event tracked by the organization, starting in triage and progressing through declared, mitigated, resolved, closed states.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.
Unique. And we never delete incidents, which becomes relevant later.

object_types.name: IncidentNumber
object_types.definition: The unique identifier of an incident, formatted as INC- followed by a sequence.

object_types.definition: A notification raised by the monitoring platform (or manually by an engineer) indicating a potential incident.

object_types.name: Ticket
object_types.definition: A support ticket raised by or on behalf of a customer, potentially linked to an incident.

object_types.name: TicketNumber

object_types.name: Severity
object_types.definition: The technical blast-radius classification of an incident, ranging from SEV1 (everything down for everyone) to SEV4 (degraded, cosmetic, localized).

source_references.excerpt: SEV1 through SEV4. It's about blast radius and technical impact. SEV1 is everything's down for everyone. SEV4 is degraded, cosmetic, one region, nobody's really suffering.

object_types.name: Priority
object_types.definition: The customer-urgency classification of an incident, independent of severity, ranging from P1 to P4.

source_references.excerpt: And priority is P1 through P4.
Priority is about customer urgency. Who's affected, what they've promised their own customers, whether we're breaching an SLA.

object_types.name: IncidentState
object_types.definition: The current lifecycle state of an incident.

object_types.name: Person
object_types.definition: An individual who may serve as incident commander.

object_types.name: Team
object_types.definition: A group that owns a service on a standing basis.

source_references.excerpt: A team. Services are owned by teams. People move.

object_types.name: Service
object_types.definition: A system or product component that can be affected by incidents and is owned by exactly one team.

ambiguities.description: Commander is modeled as a Person identified by name, but no explicit identifier scheme (e.g., employee ID) was discussed -- only 'named' was mentioned. Is person_name a reliable unique identifier, or is there a separate employee ID system?

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

ambiguities.description: Severity and Priority mandatory rules are described as applying only once an incident is 'declared'; triage incidents may lack values. The current model marks these mandatory at the Incident role level, but this is only accurate for declared incidents. Should Severity/Priority mandatory constraints be scoped by state (e.g., via subtyping Declared Incident from Incident)?

source_references.excerpt: Every declared incident has a severity. That's mandatory, you can't declare without one.
A commander is assigned when it's declared... Declared incidents have exactly one commander. Triage incidents have none.

ambiguities.description: The term 'owner' is overloaded: it refers both to the incident commander (temporary role) and the service owner (standing team assignment). The transcript explicitly flags this as a source of confusion in day-to-day communication ('who owns this?'). Modelers/users should be careful to disambiguate in any UI or reporting that uses the word 'owner'.

source_references.excerpt: Nadia: There is, and it's the second collision. The service owner is the team that owns the broken thing... Owen: And in a channel, 'who owns this?' means either. It's genuinely ambiguous every single time.

ambiguities.description: Severity and priority can change over time (revised as blast radius is understood), and history is kept 'in the timeline, as events' -- a separate mechanism not modeled here. Should the timeline/event history be modeled explicitly as a fact type, or is capturing only current severity/priority sufficient for this model's purpose?

source_references.excerpt:
Can either change during the incident?
Nadia: Constantly. Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius. That's normal and expected.
...
In the timeline, as events. The incident record carries the current severity.

ambiguities.description: The classification of incidents later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration (e.g., for exclusion from reliability metrics) is explicitly undecided and parked pending a decision from Ravi. No 'cause classification' concept is included in the model per the facilitator's explicit statement.

source_references.excerpt:
Facilitator: Is there a decision here today?
Kit: No, and it's above all three of us... Parking it explicitly, then. Whether an incident later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left as-is, is undecided.

ambiguities.description: The 'monitoring' state mentioned by Owen is explicitly excluded from the model because it is not in the system's dropdown, despite being informally treated as a state by some staff. This is a known discrepancy between informal practice and the system of record.

source_references.excerpt:
Owen: There's also "monitoring," which sits between mitigated and resolved.
Nadia: That's not a state, that's a thing people write in the channel.
...
Facilitator: If it's not in the system I'm not modelling it. Five states.

ambiguities.description: The acyclic/no-chain rule for incident duplicates is stated as the intended rule but explicitly 'not enforced' in the system today. Should this be modeled as a hard constraint (which would misrepresent current data, since two-deep chains have been observed) or as a soft/aspirational rule?
